prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- President Bush has expressed his "deep concern" and regret to Iraq's prime minister over the desecration of a Quran by an American soldier, the White House said Tuesday. President Bush called Nuri al-Maliki over the incident, al-Maliki's office says. The leaders are seen in September. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said Bush spoke to Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Monday in one of their regularly scheduled secure video teleconferences. "President Bush expressed his deep concern over the incident and told Prime Minister Maliki that the soldier has been reprimanded by his commanders and removed from Iraq," Johndroe said. Al-Maliki's office on Tuesday said Bush issued an apology for the action on behalf of the United States and "promised to present the soldier to the courts." The office said Bush made the apology in a call to al-Maliki on Tuesday morning. An American staff sergeant -- a sniper section leader -- used a Quran for target practice in Iraq earlier this month. The U.S. commander in Baghdad issued a formal apology Saturday and read a letter of apology by the shooter.  Watch the U.S. military formally apologize » . The sergeant has been relieved of duty as a section leader "with prejudice," officially reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment and redeployed -- reassigned to the United States, the U.S. military said. Reports of the Quran desecration have enraged Muslims in Iraq and elsewhere around the world. The soldier, whose name was not released, shot at a Quran on May 9, villagers said. The Quran used in the incident was discovered two days later, according to the military. A tribal leader said "the criminal act by U.S. forces" took place at a shooting range at the Radhwaniya police station on Baghdad's western outskirts. After the shooters left, an Iraqi policeman found a target marked in the middle of the bullet-riddled Quran. Pictures of the Quran show multiple bullet holes and an expletive scrawled on one of its pages. Officials said the soldier asserted he wasn't aware the book was the Quran, but U.S. officials rejected the claim. On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, appeared with leaders from Radhwaniya and apologized. "I come before you here seeking your forgiveness," Hammond said to tribal leaders and others at the ceremony. "In the most humble manner I look in your eyes today and I say please forgive me and my soldiers." Hammond also read a letter from the shooter, who called his actions "shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible," but he insisted he was not being malicious. "I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together," the letter said. Hammond said the soldier's actions were tantamount to "criminal behavior." "I've come to this land to protect you, to support you -- not to harm you -- and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable," the general said. Another military official kissed a Quran and presented it as "a humble gift" to the tribal leaders. Many Iraqi leaders said the apology alone would not suffice.  Watch villagers protest the desecration » . On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, the movement of Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, condemned what it said was a "blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world." The party said it reacted to the news "with deep resentment and indignation" and wants the "severest of punishments" for the action. "What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers," al-Hashimi said. "I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future." CNN's Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

Bush called al-Maliki regarding the incident, according to the prime minister’s office. The two leaders are pictured together in September.

National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said Bush spoke with al-Maliki on Monday during one of their regularly scheduled secure video teleconferences.

“President Bush expressed his deep concern over the incident and told Prime Minister Maliki that the soldier has been reprimanded by his commanders and removed from Iraq,” Johndroe said.

Al-Maliki’s office said Tuesday that Bush apologized for the act on behalf of the United States and “promised to present the soldier to the courts.” According to the office, Bush made the apology during a call to al-Maliki on Tuesday morning.

An American staff sergeant—a sniper section leader—used a Quran for target practice in Iraq earlier this month. On Saturday, the U.S. commander in Baghdad issued a formal apology and read a letter of apology from the shooter.

Watch the U.S. military formally apologize »

The sergeant was relieved of his duties as a section leader “with prejudice,” formally reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment, and redeployed—reassigned to the United States—the U.S. military said.

Reports of the Quran’s desecration have enraged Muslims in Iraq and elsewhere around the world.

Villagers said the soldier, whose name was not released, shot at a Quran on May 9. According to the military, the Quran used in the incident was discovered two days later.

A tribal leader said “the criminal act by U.S. forces” occurred at a shooting range at the Radhwaniya police station on Baghdad’s western outskirts. After the shooters left, an Iraqi police officer found a target marked in the center of the bullet-riddled Quran.

Photographs of the Quran show multiple bullet holes and an expletive scrawled across one of its pages.

Officials said the soldier maintained that he had not known the book was the Quran, but U.S. officials rejected that claim.

On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, appeared alongside leaders from Radhwaniya and apologized.

“I come before you here seeking your forgiveness,” Hammond told tribal leaders and others attending the ceremony. “In the most humble manner, I look in your eyes today and I say please forgive me and my soldiers.”

Hammond also read a letter from the shooter, who described his actions as “shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible” but insisted that he had not acted maliciously.

“I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together,” the letter said.

Hammond said the soldier’s actions were tantamount to “criminal behavior.”

“I’ve come to this land to protect you, to support you—not to harm you—and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable,” the general said.

Another military official kissed a Quran and presented it to the tribal leaders as “a humble gift.”

Many Iraqi leaders said the apology alone was insufficient.

Watch villagers protest the desecration »

On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, the movement of Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, condemned what it described as a “blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world.”

The party said it had received the news “with deep resentment and indignation” and called for the “severest of punishments” for the act.

“What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers,” al-Hashimi said.

“I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second, a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future.”

CNN’s Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The White House said Tuesday that President Bush conveyed profound concern and regret to Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki after a U.S. soldier desecrated a Quran.

According to National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe, Bush discussed the episode with al-Maliki on Monday during one of the leaders’ routinely scheduled secure video conferences. The two leaders had previously been pictured together in September.

Johndroe said Bush informed the Iraqi prime minister that the serviceman had been formally disciplined by his commanders and transferred out of Iraq.

Al-Maliki’s office offered a somewhat different account Tuesday, saying Bush apologized on behalf of the United States and pledged that the soldier would be brought before the courts. It said the apology came during a telephone conversation with al-Maliki on Tuesday morning.

The soldier, an American staff sergeant who led a sniper section, used a copy of the Quran for shooting practice in Iraq earlier this month. On Saturday, the U.S. commander in Baghdad formally apologized and publicly read a written apology from the serviceman. Video showed the U.S. military making the formal apology.

The military said the staff sergeant was removed from his position as section leader “with prejudice,” officially reprimanded by his commanding general, expelled from his regiment and redeployed to the United States.

News of the Quran’s desecration provoked outrage among Muslims in Iraq and around the world.

Villagers said the unnamed soldier fired at the holy book on May 9. The military reported that the damaged Quran was found two days afterward.

A tribal leader said the “criminal act by U.S. forces” occurred at a firing range at the Radhwaniya police station on the western edge of Baghdad. Once the shooters had departed, an Iraqi police officer discovered a target placed in the center of the bullet-pierced Quran.

Photographs showed numerous bullet holes in the book, along with an obscenity written across one of its pages.

Officials said the serviceman claimed he had not realized the book was a Quran, but U.S. authorities did not accept that explanation.

Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, who commanded American forces in Baghdad, appeared Saturday alongside Radhwaniya leaders and asked for forgiveness.

Addressing tribal leaders and other people attending the ceremony, Hammond said he had come before them to seek their pardon. He added that, with the greatest humility, he was looking them in the eyes and asking them to forgive both him and his troops.

Hammond also read a statement written by the shooter. In it, the soldier described his conduct as lacking foresight, extremely reckless and irresponsible, while maintaining that he had not acted with malicious intent.

The letter said the soldier sincerely hoped his behavior had not damaged the partnership built by the two countries.

Hammond characterized the serviceman’s conduct as equivalent to criminal behavior. The general said his purpose in Iraq was to protect and assist Iraqis rather than hurt them, and he called the soldier’s actions entirely wrong and unacceptable.

During the event, another military officer kissed a Quran and gave it to the tribal leaders as “a humble gift.”

A video also showed villagers demonstrating against the desecration.

Numerous Iraqi officials said an apology by itself was inadequate.

On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, which is associated with Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, denounced the episode as a “blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world.”

The party said it received the report with profound anger and indignation and demanded the harshest possible punishment.

Al-Hashimi said the principal concern was that such offenses had occurred repeatedly, citing earlier incidents in which mosques were destroyed and U.S. troops tore pages from the Quran and used them in degrading ways.

He said he had requested, first, that the apology be entered into the official record and, second, that the U.S. military guarantee the strongest punishment available for the soldier so the penalty would discourage other troops from committing similar acts.

CNN’s Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to the report.

During a telephone call, Bush assured Maliki that the incident did not reflect American values and promised that those responsible would be held accountable. The Iraqi government said Bush had apologized and pledged that appropriate legal action would be taken.

The Quran, which had been placed on a shooting range and riddled with bullets, was discovered by Iraqi police in the Radwaniyah area west of Baghdad. The incident quickly provoked anger among Iraqi officials, religious leaders, and members of the public, who regarded the treatment of Islam’s holy book as a grave insult. Demonstrations were held, and some Iraqi leaders warned that the episode could damage cooperation between the United States and Iraq.

Senior U.S. military officers issued a formal apology to local tribal and community leaders. At a public meeting, an American commander condemned the soldier’s actions, presented a new copy of the Quran, and emphasized that the U.S. military respected Islam. Military officials said the act was committed by one soldier and did not represent the attitudes or policies of American forces in Iraq.

The soldier, a staff sergeant assigned to a sniper unit, was formally reprimanded. He was removed from his leadership position, taken out of his regiment, and reassigned to the United States. Officials also said he had apologized and maintained that he had not initially realized the target was a Quran.

Despite the disciplinary measures and repeated apologies, the desecration generated widespread outrage across the Muslim world. The controversy intensified Iraqi suspicion of the American military and placed additional strain on already sensitive U.S.-Iraqi relations at a time when both governments were negotiating the future role of U.S. forces in the country.
